name: MOTS-c

lead: MOTS-c is a short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that rises with exercise. Users run it in peptide stacks as an exercise mimetic to burn fat, build endurance and reverse age-related decline, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs.

In mice it promoted metabolic balance and reduced obesity and insulin resistance, acting on the folate-methionine cycle and AMPK, and it moves to the nucleus under stress to influence gene expression. Human data are limited to observational studies of circulating levels, early-phase studies of a synthetic analogue and a registered phase 2 trial in prediabetes.

paras: Sold as a research chemical, discussed in peptide-stacking communities in cycled courses combined with training and diet. Product identity and purity are not independently verified.
Human safety data for vendor products are essentially absent. It is not an approved drug and has been named as prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency since 2024; gray-market purity is unreliable.

angle.text: MOTS-c is used as an exercise mimetic that users hope improves glucose and fat metabolism for a leaner body, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs. Findings so far are from mice, with little human data on appearance.

lead: MOTS-c (mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c) is a 16-amino-acid peptide, with the sequence MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR, encoded in humans by the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 gene.[1] It belongs to the mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), short peptides encoded by small open reading frames in mitochondrial DNA, of which eight have been identified.[2] It is believed to take part in the regulation of glucose metabolism by skeletal muscle, rises with exercise, and is described as an exercise mimetic.[1][3]

A team led by Changhan Lee in Pinchas Cohen's laboratory at the University of Southern California described it in 2015 in Cell Metabolism, reporting in mice that it promoted metabolic homeostasis and reduced obesity and insulin resistance.[1][4] Later work linked it to physical fitness, reduced obesity and longer healthy lifespan in mice, and showed that it moves to the cell nucleus under metabolic stress to influence gene expression.[1][5][6]

MOTS-c is not approved to treat any medical condition. The World Anti-Doping Agency named it explicitly as prohibited beginning in 2024, and Wikipedia reports its use as an injectable supplement within a "peptide stacking" trend despite the lack of robust human data.[1] Published human data are limited to observational studies of circulating levels and exercise responses, with early-phase studies of a synthetic analogue and a registered phase 2 trial in prediabetes.[7][8][9]
infobox: Not approved for any use; prohibited by WADA (explicitly from 2024); sold as a research chemical

paras: According to Grokipedia, MOTS-c has a molecular weight of about 2,174.6 g/mol and was found through an in silico screen of short open reading frames in the human mitochondrial genome, following the earlier discovery of the mitochondrial-derived peptide humanin in 2001.[10] The 2015 paper identified a 51-base-pair open reading frame in the 12S rRNA gene and validated its mitochondrial origin through depleting mitochondrial DNA in cells.[10][4] The peptide is highly conserved in its N-terminal residues and has been detected in plasma of humans and rodents, suggesting an endocrine-like role.[10] Wikipedia notes that MOTS-c binds casein kinase 2.[1]

Reviews describe MOTS-c as acting on skeletal muscle and adipose metabolism, enhancing insulin sensitivity and glucose utilisation.[11][12] Proposed mechanisms include effects on the folate and methionine cycle, activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), and, under metabolic stress, translocation to the nucleus where it regulates nuclear gene expression.[5][10][9] A 2021 Nature Communications paper described MOTS-c as an exercise-induced mitochondrial-encoded regulator of age-dependent physical decline and muscle homeostasis in mice.[6] MOTS-c levels have been reported to be lower in diabetes and to rise after exercise,[10][13][14] and a study in the Journal of Applied Physiology reported that acute endurance exercise raised circulating levels of mitochondrial-derived peptides in humans.[7] Whether injected synthetic MOTS-c reproduces these effects in people has not been shown in published controlled trials.

Laboratory research has examined MOTS-c in metabolic disease, ageing, cancer and the senescence process. Reviews cover the peptide's therapeutic prospects,[9] its role in preventing metabolic disorders,[11] its connection with exercise,[3] and the role of mitochondrial peptides in energy metabolism and ageing.[2][15] A review titled Mitochondrial-Derived Peptides Exacerbate Senescence proposed that humanin and MOTS-c, which are hypothesised to have anti-ageing activity on the basis of correlative evidence, may need to be re-examined with regard to senescence,[16] and a separate 2018 Aging paper examined how mitochondrial peptides modulate mitochondrial function during cellular senescence.[17] A 2015 Aging Cell article asked whether MOTS-c might play a role in exceptional longevity.[18] Other reports examine effects on ovarian cancer cells in the laboratory.[19]

Grokipedia reports that an analogue, CB4211, was the first mitochondrial-derived peptide analogue to enter human trials, with a phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study initiated in 2019 for fatty liver disease; this concerns a modified drug candidate and not vendor MOTS-c.[10]

No published randomised trial has tested injected MOTS-c for fat loss, endurance, longevity or appearance outcomes in humans. Human research to date measures endogenous MOTS-c levels. A randomised trial examined the effect of aerobic and resistance exercise on MOTS-c in Hispanic and non-Hispanic white breast cancer survivors,[20] another reported circulating MOTS-c in breast cancer patients treated with metformin,[21] and trials examined acute endurance exercise and levels of mitochondrial peptides in humans,[7] and heat stress effects on MOTS-c and FGF21 during calf immobilisation in active men.[22] Another study examined mitochondrial-derived peptide C with beta-amyloid as predictors of adverse outcome in type 2 diabetics with coronary disease.[23] A 2026 sports-medicine review of approved and unapproved peptide therapies for musculoskeletal injury and athletic performance discusses the rapidly expanding use of peptides.[24]

Registered trials include a phase 2 study of MOTS-c to improve insulin sensitivity in adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity (n=120, recruiting, started February 2026),[8] observational studies of MOTS-c in type 2 diabetes with coronary disease,[25] and a study of anaesthesia types and levels of ferroptosis markers, humanin and MOTS-c in kidney transplantation.[26]

Human safety data for vendor MOTS-c are essentially absent. Products are sold as research chemicals without regulatory oversight, so identity and purity are not independently verified; Grokipedia notes that suppliers advertise purities of 98 percent or above with analytical certification, but those claims are not independently checked.[10] WADA and USADA classify it as prohibited because of potential performance enhancement without an established medical use.[1][10]

In 2025 and 2026 T Nation threads, MOTS-c appears in peptide lists. Members mention it among compounds ranked for weight loss, alongside CJC-1295, ipamorelin, SS-31 and others,[27] ask whether to use it in preference to 5-amino-1MQ or AOD-9604 when trying to reach a lower body-fat level on a GLP-1 type drug,[28] and report including it in stacks with growth hormone secretagogues, testosterone and retatrutide.[29][30] One poster dismisses GLP-1 drugs as only for those with no discipline and lists MOTS-c among preferred weight loss peptides.[31] A separate thread includes a video titled around ranking peptides including MOTS-c.[32] These are user posts and not clinical data, and no looksmax.org or Reddit material was identified.

lore.intro: On T Nation MOTS-c is treated as a fat-loss and metabolic peptide alongside GH secretagogues and GLP-1 drugs, mainly in 2025 and 2026 posts by people discussing stacks.[27][28][29]

timeline.event: Humanin, the first mitochondrial-derived peptide, is identified, per Grokipedia.[10]
MOTS-c is reported in Cell Metabolism by a USC team; it reduces obesity and insulin resistance in mice.[4]
MOTS-c is shown to translocate to the nucleus and regulate nuclear gene expression under metabolic stress.[5]
Phase 1 trial of analogue CB4211 starts for fatty liver disease, per Grokipedia.[10]
MOTS-c is described as an exercise-induced regulator of age-dependent physical decline in mice.[6]
Phase 2 trial in prediabetes with overweight or obesity begins recruiting.[8]
